locally frequent and conspicuous plant in the north and 
west, occurring as dense cushions in small crevices and 
hollows on the tops of dry, sun-exposed or slightly shaded, 
acid or mildly basic rocks, often where there is a thin 
cover of humus. It is found on slate, schist, gabbro, basalt, 
peridotite, granite and sandstone but is largely absent from 
limestone. Typical habitats are detached angular boulders 
and granite tors, stone walls, bridges, Cornish hedges 
and roadside rocks. Frullania tamarisci, Hedwigia stellata, 
Hypnum cupressiforme, Racomitrium aciculare, R. fasciculare, 
R. heterostichum and R. lanuginosum are common associates. 
It also occurs occasionally in old quarries and on mine waste, 
on coastal rocks, and on dry boulders in lightly shaded areas 
in wooded valleys. Near the southern and eastern edge of 
its range it is more often found in man-made habitats than 
on natural rock outcrops, even colonising railway ballast in 
Oceanic Southern-temperate. W Europe, from Portugal and 
Corsica north to the Faeroes and SW Norway, east to 
S Sweden, Slovenia and Croatia. Azores, Canaries, Madeira.

The postfertilization fusion between the carpogonium and hypogynous cells has been variously reported in Grateloupia species (Kawabata, 1962; Kraft, 1977; Kawaguchi et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2000; de Clerck et al., 2005) and denied in Grateloupia indica, Grateloupia comorinii, Grateloupia lithophila (Balakrishnan, 1961), and G. filicina (Baweja and Sahoo, 2002).
Grateloupia growing in the intertidal region possess a discoid holdfast for firm anchorage when inhabiting stagnant brackish waters, eg, Chilika Lake (Baweja and Sahoo, 2002). Growth in Grateloupia is multiaxial and is initiated by a group of apical cells; thalli are differentiated into cortex and medulla. The cortex is further divided into outer cortex and inner cortex. The cortex is 6–10 layered and the medulla is lax, composed of interwoven stellate cells. The medullary filaments provide strength and flexibility to the plant. A thick layer of extracellular mucilage veneers the thallus of Grateloupia lithophila. This mucilage is a mixture of insoluble, carboxylated, and sulfated polysaccharides (Baweja, 2005).

The species of Grateloupia is dioecious with male plants smaller and narrower as compared to female or tetrasporic plants. Plants are found growing throughout the year. However, the percentage of the cystocarpic fronds decreases from February to September. The female plants are distinguished morphologically and the male and tetrasporic plants cannot be distinguished. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Class Florideophyceae  Order Halymeniales  Family Halymeniaceae     
Grateloupia dichotoma J. Agardh  
Morphology
Thallus flat, dark-brown, basal part cuneiform, with 
short cylindrical stem, to 7 cm high, attachment to 
substrate with holdfast; branching regularly or irregu-
larly dichotomous; branches linear, linear-cuneated or 
lance-oblong, 0.5–2 mm wide, with blunt or pointed 
apices often arranged at same level; laterals may 
develop on both sides of branches. 
Ecology/habitat
On stones, rocks, artificial substrata, to 10 m deep, 
mainly in extremely wave-exposed sites, epilithic; 
perennial, peak of vegetation from late summer 
to early autumn; recorded from some locations of 
Ukrainian, Russian and Turkish coast. 
Commercial & 
possible use
Plants of Grateloupia dichotoma provide the source 
of agar, vitamins B and E (thiamine, riboflavin, 
α-tocopherol), pantothenic and nicotine acids, mine­
ral salts, antihelmintic and antitumor BASs; a food-
stuff in some Asian countries.

# Grateloupia filicina (J.V. Lamouroux) C. Agardh

Description: Compressed, tufted, dark purplish brown fronds, to 120 mm high, main axis 1-4 mm broad. Once or twice pinnate, axes and branchlets tapered at base and apex.
Habitat: On rock in pools. mid-intertidal to shallow subtidal, sporadic, often locally common; SW England and Wales, S and W Ireland north to Donegal.
Similar species: Plants known as Grateloupia filicina var. luxurians A. & E. S. Gepp, found on pebbles and shells in open muddy and sandy estuarine habitats in Hampshire and Dorset, are now referred to as Grateloupia subpectinata Holmes. This entity, which is very much larger than Grateloupia filicina var. filicina at up to 500 mm in length represents an immigrant, perhaps of Australian origin, the first European record of which was from the Isle of Wight, in 1949. It is likely to have been introduced into harbour areas in Australia, Brittany, Spain, and Mediterranean France, probably from Japan.
